fields.sections.0.h: Major Update in a Decade, Beginning of a New Era
fields.sections.1.h: Simplified Navigation, Focus on Three Core Areas
fields.sections.2.h: Evolution of Discovery Experience, Smart Recommendations Without Tracking
fields.sections.3.h: Enhanced Search and Filtering, Expanded Multilingual Support
fields.sections.4.h: Fundamental Improvement in Installation Experience, Positive Impact of EU Regulations
fields.sections.5.h: Automatic Updates as Default, Maintaining Fine-Grained Control Options
fields.sections.6.h: Security and Privacy, Support for Users in Vulnerable Environments
fields.sections.7.h: Simplified App Hiding Feature, Enhanced User Understanding of Limitations
fields.sections.8.h: Flexibility Maintained for Custom Android like CalyxOS
fields.sections.9.h: Modernization of Internal Architecture, Establishing Long-term Maintenance Foundation
fields.sections.0.ko: F-Droid released version 2.0 after more than a year of development, which is a complete redesign of the official app and the largest update in a decade. The existing F-Droid has helped users discover and install free and open-source Android apps for over 10 years. Version 2.0 provides a simple and intuitive experience for both new and existing users through a modern interface, improved app discovery experience, and enhanced search functionality. Beyond simple design improvements, the entire user experience has been redesigned to align with modern Android patterns like Material Design, and core components have been rewritten in Kotlin Compose, establishing a foundation for rapid future improvements.
fields.sections.1.ko: One of the major goals of 2.0 was to make app discovery, installation, and management easier. The main navigation has been simplified into three core areas: Discover, Search, and My Apps. Categories are now integrated into Discover so users can explore more easily, and My Apps provides a single place to manage installed apps, updates, and potential issues. Settings and Nearby Swap functionality are still accessible with one tap in the top bar, but no longer occupy main navigation space. This structural improvement was designed to allow users to quickly access needed functions while reducing interface complexity.
fields.sections.2.ko: As the F-Droid ecosystem grew to thousands of apps, finding the right app became increasingly difficult, and addressing this was a major goal of 2.0. The improved Discover screen highlights not only newly added and recently updated apps but also the most downloaded apps in the repository. The category system has been significantly expanded and refined, with more granular categories added such as VPN, firewall, password manager, launcher, and navigation tools, making it easier to find specific types of apps. In particular, the game category has been completely reworked, dividing all games into 17 different game genres instead of grouping them in one place, making it much easier for users to find games they actually enjoy. All these improvements are achieved without tracking users or attempting to increase app usage time.
fields.sections.3.ko: Search has been improved to search not only app names but also app descriptions, categories, and translated content, allowing users to find apps by functionality rather than name. Support for CJK character systems has been significantly enhanced for Chinese, Japanese, and Korean users so they can find apps more accurately in their own language. Search remembers recent search queries, so users don't need to type the same search from scratch next time. Additionally, powerful filtering options have been added that allow multiple conditions such as app category, device compatibility, and anti-features to be combined to precisely narrow down a large app list to what is desired. For example, users can choose to see only action games compatible with their device while simultaneously excluding apps that rely on private network services.
fields.sections.4.ko: For a long time, Android restricted the app installation and update experience compared to third-party app stores like F-Droid. However, due to pressure from the EU's Digital Markets Act (DMA) and global antitrust measures, all app stores can now provide smoother and more automated installation and update experiences. F-Droid 2.0 performed groundbreaking work utilizing these new capabilities, using integrated installer across all F-Droid installations, whether included by default in the operating system or installed directly. The integrated installer leverages new pre-approved APIs, so on supported devices users can confirm immediately after deciding to install rather than after the app is downloaded. This brings the F-Droid installation experience on official Android devices much closer to what the built-in app store provides.
fields.sections.5.ko: F-Droid 2.0 has now changed to automatically fetch and install app updates by default, but respects existing settings of users who want more control. In the past, many users checked for updates from all repositories with a pull-to-refresh gesture, but in 2.0 this gesture is restricted to scrolling only. Instead, the app can now check for updates automatically in the background, so users no longer need to manually tap refresh. Nevertheless, for users who want more control, fine-grained manual update options are still provided and can be accessed from the action overflow menu (three dots) on the My Apps screen. These settings have been redesigned to be intuitively adjustable to meet the needs of diverse global users, from those with affordable data access to users in very expensive regions, those with high privacy requirements, and those using limited devices.
fields.sections.6.ko: F-Droid has long included privacy and security features to support users in vulnerable environments where installing certain apps or using F-Droid itself can attract attention. Tor is a major privacy tool, and F-Droid has long supported using Tor for all network connections and using Tor onion services for repositories and mirrors. However, the way Tor is integrated into Android has changed significantly (with various options like TorVPN, Orbot, TorServices), so settings have been simplified and unreliable auto-detection has been removed. Users who previously had 「Use Tor」 enabled will be migrated to regular proxy settings, and in the future regular Tor VPN is recommended with proxy settings left for users requiring manual control. Additionally, 'panic button' features that allow users to quickly remove sensitive information from their device in emergencies continue to be included.
fields.sections.7.ko: F-Droid was a pioneer in providing app hiding features for privacy, including a 'panic' feature that disguises the F-Droid app as a simple calculator app. Subsequently, Orbot, TorVPN, Signal and others also added these masking features, and standard design formed among widely used apps. In 2.0, this standard design was adopted, but the feature was simplified so users understand the limitations of masking precisely. Instead of the mask appearing and functioning as a simple calculator, now only the app icon and name are affected, so users understand that the F-Droid app will still be visible in the 'Apps' section of device settings and can be detected by forensic examination. Meanwhile, in response to panic trigger apps like Ripple, the ability to remove and initialize apps has not yet returned. While acknowledging this feature is important for privacy and personal protection, it was determined that maintenance requires professional work and the user base is small enough that it cannot hinder many other important improvements. Users dependent on this feature can defer updating to 2.0 while the development team evaluates whether to restore the feature.
fields.sections.8.ko: F-Droid was designed to be integrated into any version of Android or AOSP, such as CalyxOS, emteriaOS, iodéOS, Lineage-for-microG, and ShiftOS. Each operating system can include its own repository by default using an 'additional repositories' mechanism, and these repositories are displayed in the user's repository overview. However, F-Droid Privileged Extension (FPE) is currently not supported in 2.0, and even if FPE is installed, F-Droid 2.0 will not use it. The major improvements in 2.0 focused on full feature support for Android's 'SessionInstaller', which enables background updates on all recent Android versions without FPE.
fields.sections.9.ko: While many improvements in F-Droid 2.0 are visible on the surface, the most important changes happened in the inconspicuous background. All new code in this work follows modern Android development practices, establishing a foundation for faster and more stable feature improvements in the future. While the source appears to be in incomplete state, the development team plans to gradually roll out 2.0 to users over the coming weeks after 14 test releases.
fields.caveat: The source appears to be in incomplete state, and since it is F-Droid's own explanation of technical achievements and philosophy, independent verification is necessary.
